newsitem.title: USA: U.S. airlines have little room for BA passengers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. airlines have little room for BA passengers.

text.p: U.S. airlines said they will try to help passengers and cargo stranded by the cabin crew strike at British Airways Plc but warned that there was limited extra space during the hectic summer travel season.
"We are accommodating some customers. But this is the very busy travel season internationally; there's a minimal amount of seats available," said Bill Berry, a spokesman for Delta Air Lines Inc.

Delta and UAL Corp's United Airlines each said they will try to accept BA passengers for any empty seats. The airlines said they did not plan to add extra flights, since their fleets and crews were already being fully used.

American Airlines, BA's intended alliance partner, said it will add one extra daily flight from New York's Kennedy Airport to London Heathrow on Wednesday through Friday. American, a unit of AMR Corp, normally offers four daily flights from Kennedy to Heathrow.
British airline Virgin Atlantic Airways, a unit of Virgin York and London on July 11.
BA grounded half of its flights out of London and about 20 to 30 percent of its flights worldwide after the Transport and General Workers' Union went on strike Wednesday morning.

"It's a pretty significant disruption when you look at BA's market share. There could be a lot of concern and disruption on those transatlantic routes," said Ethan Simon, a spokesman for Woodside Travel Trust, a partnership of more than 130 travel agencies.
Despite the cabin crew strike in London, there was no work stoppage by BA employees at Kennedy Airport or anywhere in the United States, said John Lampl, a BA spokesman in New York.
"There is no problem from anybody anywhere in the U.S.," said BA spokesman John Lampl. "Everyone is working normally."
Lampl said the strike is "pretty invisible" at Kennedy, although he said there are "a couple" of picketers at the terminal.
